web_title: 3. Distribution, Supply Chain & Unit Economics Waterfall
book_title: Chapter 3: Inside the Machine — Supply Chain, Distribution & Unit Economics
question: How does Arista build and distribute its switches without owning factories, what are its silicon and inventory bottlenecks, and how does $100 of revenue convert to free cash flow?

epigraph.quote: Amateurs talk strategy; professionals study logistics.
epigraph.author: General Omar Bradley (attributed)

web_blocks.title: 3.1 Dual-Track Distribution: Direct Hyperscale Engineering vs. Channel VARs

web_blocks.html: Arista runs a lean, two-track sales model. That setup kept Sales & Marketing at just 5.9% of FY2025 revenue, or $533.4 million on $9,005.7 million [1][5]. For Cloud and AI Titans, a single win at Microsoft or Meta can bring in hundreds of millions each year. Arista sells directly to these giants through senior systems engineers [1][9]. Those engineers co-design rack layouts, cooling limits, and EOS telemetry hooks alongside customer teams [9]. Hyperscaler qualification takes 9 to 18 months of lab tests, burn-in runs, and software checks. Once qualified, those steep engineering hurdles protect Arista from new rivals.

Enterprise and Campus buyers (32% of sales) and Specialty Providers (20%) use a different path [1]. Here, Arista pairs direct account reps with Value-Added Resellers (VARs), system integrators, and Managed Service Providers (MSPs) [1]. Channel partners handle local delivery, multi-site staging, and regional credit in EMEA (11.9% of FY2025 sales; 11.2% in 9M 2026) and APAC (9.0% in FY2025; 7.9% in 9M 2026) [1][2][7]. Notably, Note 1 of the FY2025 Form 10-K reveals a hidden channel credit concentration: Arista's top two resellers accounted for 52% of total accounts receivable at December 31, 2025 (up from 50% at year-end 2024), concentrating collection exposure on $2,327.8 million of net receivables as of Q3 2026 [1][2]. This partner network lets Arista serve the globe with just 5,115 employees [1].

Arista owns zero chip fabs and zero assembly plants. It outsources production to Electronic Manufacturing Services (EMS) partners—mainly Jabil Inc., Sanmina Corporation, and Foxconn Hon Hai, plus Flex Ltd. in some periods [1]. These factories operate in Malaysia, Vietnam, and Mexico [1]. Staying asset-light kept FY2025 capital spending at just $119.5 million, or 1.3% of revenue [1].

Avoiding factory capex creates a sharp trade-off: heavy reliance on single-source merchant silicon without long-term supply guarantees. Arista depends predominantly on Broadcom for Tomahawk (Tomahawk 5 and upcoming 102.4 Tbps Tomahawk 6) and Jericho (Jericho3-AI) chips [1][10][11]. Crucially, Note 1 and Item 1 of the FY2025 Form 10-K disclose that Arista has no guaranteed supply contracts or exclusive rights with Broadcom or its three primary contract manufacturing partners—and Broadcom simultaneously sells the exact same Tomahawk merchant silicon to white-box ODM rivals such as Celestica and Accton [1]. Arista also relies on high-speed optical transceivers, HBM/packet-buffer memory, and circuit boards manufactured across Malaysia, Vietnam, and Mexico, exposing product COGS to escalating U.S. tariffs and component inflation [1][2]. To lock in wafer and assembly slots for 800G AI ramps, Arista signs binding, non-cancellable purchase orders and posts upfront cash deposits: deposits to contract manufacturers nearly tripled (+188%) from $53.0 million at year-end 2025 to $152.8 million at September 30, 2026, while off-balance-sheet purchase commitments jumped from $6.8 billion to $11.4 billion ($9.3 billion due within 12 months) [1][2]. On-balance-sheet inventory also climbed to $3,209.8 million, including $874.3 million of evaluation gear sitting at customer sites [2]. In FY2025, Arista recorded $131.6 million in inventory write-downs inside product cost (down from $267.2 million in FY2024) [1]; if cloud specs or tariffs shift faster than buffer stock turns, excess parts can quickly erode product gross margins (already down 150 bps YoY in 9M 2026) [1][2].

web_blocks.takeaway: Out of every $100.00 of audited FY2025 revenue, Arista retained $64.06 in gross profit, spent $13.74 on R&D and just $7.50 combined on S&M and G&A, earned $42.82 in GAAP operating profit, and converted $47.22 into Free Cash Flow.

web_blocks.html: The FY2025 waterfall shows why Arista generates software-like cash flow. Customers pay upfront for multi-year CloudVision and TAC support contracts [1]. Those deferred revenue inflows, plus $439.2 million in non-cash stock-based pay, lifted operating cash flow to $4,371.9 million [1]. That cash flow beat GAAP net income by $860.5 million [1]. With capex taking only $1.33 per $100 of sales, Free Cash Flow hit $4,252.4 million, or 47.2% of revenue [1]. Still, cash conversion swings with working-capital timing. When Arista stocks billions in chips ahead of an AI ramp—as in 2022 and Q3 2026—inventory absorbs cash until shipments convert into receivables.

web_blocks.mechanism: During late-1990s component shortages, Cisco locked in massive non-cancellable multi-year purchase commitments with contract manufacturers and chip suppliers to protect against long lead times. When telecom and dot-com capex abruptly froze in early 2001, the virtual supply chain could not decelerate fast enough.
web_blocks.outcome_numbers: In Q3 FY2001 (ended April 28, 2001), Cisco recorded a $2.25 billion excess-inventory write-down and $1.17 billion in restructuring charges, posting a $2.69 billion GAAP net loss—its first quarterly loss in 11 years as a public company—as revenue dropped 30% sequentially from $6.75B to $4.73B.
web_blocks.lesson_for_symbol: Arista's $11.4 billion in non-cancellable purchase commitments alone represent ~78% of annualized Q3 revenue run-rate ($14.64 billion), and combined with $3.21 billion in inventory ($14.61 billion total) reach 99.8% of annualized Q3 sales. If hyperscaler AI capex pauses abruptly, non-cancellable supplier obligations can turn into painful gross-margin write-downs.

book_paragraphs: To see why Arista prints cash like a software company while shipping heavy metal switches, you and I need to trace how a switch moves from silicon wafer to data center rack. Arista owns zero semiconductor fabrication plants and zero assembly factories. Broadcom designs the switching silicon. Contract manufacturers—principally Jabil, Sanmina, and Foxconn—build the circuit boards and chassis in Malaysia, Vietnam, and Mexico.

Because Arista outsources physical manufacturing to three primary contract partners, it spent just 119.5 million dollars on capital expenditures across all of 2025—barely 1.3 percent of revenue—though CapEx more than doubled year-over-year to 184.9 million dollars in the first nine months of 2026 to fund lab and test infrastructure. Its real fixed asset is engineering talent. That asset-light model works brilliantly on the way up, but Form 10-K footnotes reveal two hidden concentrations you must watch closely: non-cancellable purchase commitments without guaranteed silicon contracts, and reseller receivables concentration.

When Broadcom chips and memory run tight, Arista holds no guaranteed long-term supply or exclusivity agreements—even as Broadcom sells the exact same Tomahawk chips to white-box rivals. Instead, Arista signs binding, non-cancellable purchase orders and posts upfront deposits with its contract manufacturers in Malaysia, Vietnam, and Mexico. By September 30, 2026, contract-manufacturer cash deposits had nearly tripled to 152.8 million dollars, off-balance-sheet purchase commitments hit 11.4 billion dollars, and on-balance-sheet inventory reached 3.21 billion dollars—including 874.3 million dollars of evaluation gear sitting at customer sites. Meanwhile, just two resellers accounted for 52 percent of year-end 2025 accounts receivable, meaning channel credit and tariff shocks cut directly into working capital.

book_subsections.title: Follow a Hundred Dollars Through the P&L
paragraphs: Walk through a hundred dollars of audited 2025 revenue with me, line by line. Out of every hundred dollars Arista billed, 35.94 dollars went to Broadcom silicon, contract manufacturers, optics, and support delivery, leaving 64.06 dollars in gross profit.

Next, Arista spent 13.74 dollars on Research and Development to keep EOS, CloudVision, and 800G Etherlink ahead of rivals. Notice what comes next: Sales and Marketing took just 5.92 dollars, and General and Administrative overhead took only 1.58 dollars. Why so lean? Because selling direct to Microsoft and Meta with small teams of elite systems engineers costs far less per revenue dollar than fielding an army of regional enterprise salespeople.

That leaves 42.82 dollars of GAAP operating profit per hundred dollars of sales. Add 4.37 dollars of interest earned on Arista's debt-free cash pile, subtract 8.20 dollars for income taxes, and you land at 38.99 dollars of GAAP net profit. Because customers pay upfront for multi-year CloudVision and TAC support contracts, cash flow from operations reached 48.55 dollars—and after 1.33 dollars of capital spending, Arista pocketed 47.22 dollars of Free Cash Flow for every hundred dollars of revenue.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: History offers a sharp warning on outsourced supply chains. In the spring of 2001, Cisco Systems held billions in non-cancellable supplier commitments when telecom spending vanished overnight. Within ninety days, Cisco wrote off 2.25 billion dollars in excess inventory and posted its first quarterly loss as a public company. Arista's 11.4 billion dollars in purchase commitments is backed by real hyperscaler demand today—but if AI capex ever hits a sudden wall, those binding orders become your number-one balance-sheet risk.

book_subsections.title: The Supply Chain Trade-Off: Fabless Agility vs. $11.4 Billion in Commitments
paragraphs: Arista owns no semiconductor fabs and operates no large assembly plants. Instead, it designs switch hardware and EOS software in-house, buys merchant silicon from Broadcom and optical components from specialized suppliers, and relies on contract manufacturers in Asia and North America to assemble finished systems. That fabless model explains why Arista needs minimal capital expenditure—just 1.1% of sales in FY2025—and generates massive free cash flow.

Yet asset-light does not mean risk-free. When hyperscalers place massive 800G AI orders with twelve-to-eighteen-month lead times for advanced silicon and memory, Arista must lock in supply far ahead of customer delivery. By Q3 2026, inventory had climbed to $3.21 billion and non-cancellable purchase commitments reached $11.4 billion—nearly double the $6.8 billion level at year-end 2025. As long as Cloud Titans take delivery on schedule, those commitments convert smoothly into high-margin revenue; if a major customer delays deployment, working capital absorbs the shock first.

book_subsections.title: Following One Hundred Dollars Through the Income Statement
paragraphs: Take $100 of Arista revenue in FY2025 and trace where every dollar goes. Roughly $35.94 pays for Broadcom merchant silicon, contract manufacturing, optics, and support delivery, leaving $64.06 in GAAP gross profit. From there, Arista spends $13.38 on R&D to keep EOS and 800G/1.6T platforms ahead of rivals, just $5.04 on sales and marketing because direct hyperscaler relationships require minimal ad spend, and $2.83 on general administration.

What remains is $42.81 in GAAP operating profit—a level that climbed even higher to $44.90 per $100 in Q3 2026. Add interest income earned on $14.36 billion of cash, subtract taxes, and Arista converts roughly $47.20 per $100 of FY2025 revenue into free cash flow because capital expenditures consume barely $1.10 per $100.

book_subsections.title: Why Direct Hyperscaler Selling Protects Operating Leverage
paragraphs: Most enterprise hardware vendors spend 20% to 30% of revenue on sprawling global sales forces. Arista keeps sales and marketing near 5% of revenue because hyperscalers buy directly through joint engineering roadmaps, while a lean channel partner network handles enterprise campus deals. That structural cost advantage flows straight to the bottom line.

book_subsections.title: Working Capital Velocity and Cash Conversion Mechanics
paragraphs: In hardware-heavy businesses, rapid growth usually starves cash flow because the company has to fund factories, warehouses, and receivables long before customers pay. Arista reverses that dynamic. Even as 9M 2026 revenue jumped 44.3% to $9.40 billion and inventory rose to $3.21 billion to support 800G shipments, deferred revenue climbed to $6.84 billion because hyperscale and enterprise customers pay upfront for multi-year software, support, and contracted capacity.

That upfront cash collection is why FY2025 operating cash flow of $4.37 billion exceeded GAAP net income by 24.5%. When you own a business that collects cash ahead of recognizing revenue while spending barely 1.1% of sales on capital equipment, growth creates cash rather than consuming it.

book_subsections.title: Operating Leverage as Revenue Scales Past Ten Billion
paragraphs: Look at how cleanly Arista's cost structure scales. Between FY2021 and FY2025, revenue tripled from $2.95 billion to $9.01 billion, yet research and development plus selling, general, and administrative expenses fell from roughly 29% of revenue to just 21.25%. That eight-percentage-point drop in operating overhead flowed directly into GAAP operating margins, lifting them above 42% in FY2025 and 44.9% in Q3 2026.

book_subsections.title: Hidden Supply-Chain and Receivables Fragilities in the Footnotes
paragraphs: Reading past the headline P&L into Note 1 and Note 4 of Arista's SEC filings uncovers three structural vulnerabilities that balance-sheet summaries often miss. First, Arista's three primary contract manufacturers (Jabil, Sanmina, and Foxconn) and sole predominant silicon vendor (Broadcom) operate without guaranteed supply agreements or exclusivity—meaning Arista competes for wafer allocations against the very white-box ODMs buying the same Broadcom silicon.

Second, manufacturing hubs in Malaysia, Vietnam, and Mexico expose cost of revenue to U.S. tariff shifts and memory scarcity, contributing to a 150-basis-point Product gross margin decline in the first nine months of 2026 alongside a near-tripling of upfront deposits to contract manufacturers ($152.8 million as of September 30, 2026). Third, Note 1 reveals that Arista's top two channel resellers represent 52% of total accounts receivable, creating concentrated counterparty credit risk even when end-customers are blue-chip hyperscalers.
